discovery: Optical detection and coherent control of single solid-state spins in diamond, and their use for quantum sensing
motivation: Wrachtrup and Jelezko showed that single nitrogen-vacancy defects in diamond can be detected optically, and that their electron and nuclear spins can be coherently controlled and read out at room temperature. Their work in the 1990s and 2000s turned an isolated spin in a solid from a thought experiment into a laboratory reality. Lukin, working with them and others, showed how these spins act as quantum registers and as atomic-scale magnetometers. This established nanoscale quantum sensing, which can image magnetic fields from single molecules, living cells, condensed-matter phases and geological samples. Together these advances created a new field: engineered spin defects in wide-bandgap materials, which now include silicon carbide and rare-earth hosts. These defects are used worldwide for sensing, quantum networking and entanglement distribution between distant nodes. Their work turned a fragile quantum property into a measurable, controllable and widely used technology.
